articles.summary: Slow blinking and trilling are some of the ways felines show affection – but experts say to ‘read the whole cat in context’ I talk to my cat, Blue, constantly. Because I’m obsessed with her, I like to think we have a perfect, mind-meld level of communication. But what if I’m wrong? What is Blue really trying to tell me? And what am I really telling her?
I turned to cat experts to find out how cats communicate, and how we can better understand them.

articles.title: Australian supermarket honey taste test: ‘The cheapest honey is still delicious’
articles.summary: Nicholas Jordan and a hive mind of judges tasted 27 brands of honey and found that while the best were ‘perfumed as hell’, others were as basic as reality TV. Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email. I’ve bought a lot of honey in my life.
body: I ’ve bought a lot of honey in my life. I purchased kilos of the stuff back when I used to make unmanageably large batches of bootleg muesli. But I don’t think I’ve ever purchased honey and thought about what I’m buying. I couldn’t even name the brands in my cupboard, let alone describe my thought process in choosing them.

I want to be more judicious, but how? All the ingredients are the same. There’s a huge variation in price, and I know from previous taste tests that price is a terrible predictor of deliciousness. So what should I look at? Colour? Branding? Organic certification? Specific botanicals? Where the honey comes from? It’s literally choosing a book by its cover.

I’m about as far as you can get from tech bro optimisation – I get a thrill from hitchhiking, eating unknown ingredients and being yelled at from passing cars. But this level of unpredictability and imprecision makes even me uncomfortable. The difference is, it doesn’t cost any money to be yelled at. Honey comes at a price, and I spent a lot of time acquiring those dollars, so I want to be informed when spending them.

articles.title: Korean Hair Vinegar Is the Secret to Glossy, Glass-Like Hair
articles.summary: Trying to get glass hair shine? Korean hair vinegar might be what your strands have needed this whole time. Experts explain the pH trick behind the shine, plus the formulas worth trying.
body: If we’re being honest, shiny, glass hair takes quite a bit of work. There’s the salon gloss every few weeks, the shine serum before you leave the house, and the professional blowout that never looks quite as glamorous the next morning. So when a two-minute shower step started promising the same mirror-like finish, it was bound to take off.

Enter Korean hair vinegar, which has been all over TikTok lately, with videos of dull, frizzy hair turning smooth and shiny after a single wash. It might sound like something you’d put on a salad, but the idea has deep roots. “In Korea, vinegar has always been both food and medicine,” says Ellie Byun, OMD, a doctor of Korean medicine and licensed acupuncturist.

Still, vinegar isn’t exactly the first thing you’d reach for to fix your hair, and plenty of viral trends don’t exactly live up to the hype. So does this one? Below, experts break down what hair vinegar actually does, who should try it and who should skip it, plus a few of our favorite formulas.

articles.title: Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time
articles.summary: We may earn a commission from links on this page. Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.
body: For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

body: Are the best nontoxic sunscreens just marketing speak? articles.title: When to Visit Machu Picchu for Clear Views and Fewer Crowds
articles.summary: Forget what you know about peak season—Peru's most famous site is changing. Two leading travel specialists reveal their strategies for the perfect visit in 2026.
body: You may already have a clear picture of a trip to Machu Picchu long before you have a date to go in mind. On a first visit, you want time to take in the massive scale of the Inca city on its forested ridge above the Urubamba River, and then to walk among its stone walls. That picture, of course, depends on the weather. Here, where the Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin, a single bank of cloud can hide Waynapicchu, the peak behind the ruins, and with it the panorama you came to see.

The drier months improve the odds of a clear view, but draw more visitors with similar dreams to the same routes and entry hours. The weeks just after the rains offer greener slopes—and often thinner crowds—to anyone prepared to pack for showers. The best time to visit Machu Picchu comes down to matching the conditions to the type of visit you want, as well as confirming that your route is available before you commit to booking trains and rooms. Below are the questions that first-time visitors ask most, with advice from travel advisors and experts.
